description: A group of astronomy enthusiasts, with the vision of applying our growing knowledge and curiosity to address key questions and explore new areas of space science.
summary:
This project represents a Web-tool application deployment, achieving a representation of NASA's SPHEREx infrared survey into a sky time-lapse that the user can explore. 
The application runs upon inputting a star's name or coordinates, and traverses to find every SPHEREx exposure of that patch in the sky, further extending its visualization through frame alignments.
Users can blink between visits, view a colour composite of all six detectors aboard the SPHEREx, or click on any object for its spectrum across the SPHEREx's 102 colours. 

It meets the challenge goal: easy updates to new data releases, spectra on the fly, Gaia and WISE overlays through Aladin with the flexibility of a selectable field of view.
details:
Blink Hunters is a Web app that transforms NASA's infrared survey, SPHEREx, into a time-lapse of the sky. The user enters the name of a star or its coordinates, or selects one of five test targets. The app identifies the target's current location, and adjusts the position of the catalogue entries to keep up with the rapidly moving stars without missing them, well into 2026. It then looks for all of the SPHEREx exposures of that location in NASA/IPAC's IRSA archive. Then the patches are aligned with each other on one sky grid and stacked per detector and per visit. Visitors can 'blink' between images in the browser, subtract a visitor from another, add visitors together to reveal faint objects, view a colour composite of all six images in the browser, and click on any object to display its spectrum, its brightness as a function of time and its position as a function of time. Each view will have its own web address, allowing it to be shared or hosted elsewhere.

The primary advantage is access. While SPHEREx takes photos of the entire sky every six months in 102 colours of infrared light, the same target results in hundreds of large data files, just a few of which can be used with the specialist code. Blink Hunters makes that a page that loads in seconds. It's also fair to the data: SPHEREx's filters vary the wavelength on each detector, so that users can compare visits channel by channel without confusion from changes due to colour. A saturated star is not measured badly but is flagged. The Gaia DR3 catalogue of stars and the AllWISE sky are overlaid to provide a quick context from other telescopes. When NASA's archive goes down, the five test targets continue to operate from data already programmed into the app, and targets loaded prior to this still run from saved data.

It is important that students, citizen scientists, and astronomers can use SPHEREx to find things that change or move: nearby stars, cold brown dwarfs, variable stars, and eventually, far off Solar System objects like a possible Planet X. The tool has already yielded discoveries for a astronomer to follow up. WISE 0855 is the coldest known brown dwarf, and it is located in a "pixel" with a background star, which can be distinguished by colour and motion. The young star RW Aurigae exhibited a color change on succeeding visits. We show these as candidates, rather than discoveries, like citizen-science projects such as Backyard Worlds.

The back end was developed using Python 3, FastAPI and Uvicorn as the web server. The data work relies on Astropy (coordinates, units, FITS files), astroquery and pyvo (queries on data archives), reproject (aligning images), photutils (brightness), NumPy and SciPy, and s3fs (directly reading SPHEREx data from AWS S3). The front end is HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and Aladin Lite provided by the Strasbourg Astronomical Data Center (CDS) for the interactive sky view. The data are from SPHEREx data releases DR1 and QR3 from IRSA, Gaia DR3 (from IRSA, the ESA Gaia archive and VizieR), AllWISE sky images, and CDS’s Sesame service for name lookups. The app is deployed with code on GitHub and running in Docker and is hosted on Render, and the demo datasets are built on Google Cloud Shell and deployed. Some special hardware was not required. The project discloses that we have used Claude, the AI assistant, to assist with the coding, testing and deployment.

The concept is taken from the discovery of Pluto in 1930, when someone would look at two plates of photographs and see a "blink" or "jump" on one. We made an updated version of that process for a survey that had 102 colours rather than one. There are three new things. The colour composite maps use the six detectors of SPHEREx to colour the object as red, green and blue, meaning that cold brown dwarfs appear as a reddish colour. The add/subtract mode lets users combine any visits, adding some and subtracting others, instead of always comparing with the first visit. The app reads colour and motion, too, and can distinguish two objects in one 6-arcsecond pixel. Even it marks the challenge's own initial WISE 0855 coordinates, from a previous epoch, and tracks the brown dwarf to its current location.

We designed Blink Hunters to address actual constraints of the data from SPHEREx. There are 102 wavelength bands observed by SPHEREx and it revisits each sky position approximately 6 months apart using linear variable filters. We therefore directly compared with matched wavelengths between visits, applied 6.15″ pixels and masked the 13 flag bits of bad pixels to make sure detector artefacts do not appear as real motion. Positional accuracy mattered. We calculated the proper motions of Gaia DR3 to the epoch of the observations, we ran a few Gaia mirrors to speed up our processing, and we added a backup that returned older DR2 positions around 5″ off for stars which move fast such as Barnard's Star. Judges and the public also had to have reliability. Mostly, the NASA IRSA archive returns 502 errors, so we have implemented retries, cache exposure lists, and preloaded the demo targets to still be able to use the app when the NASA IRSA archive is down. There was also the need to squeeze in the free 512 MB space limit. The app doesn't require any login or installation for usability. One click presets, colour composite using the 6 detectors, add and subtract of any two visits (not just visit 1). Aladin Lite provides familiar sky context as provided by WISE and 2MASS.
